articles.title: Report: US considering a $100,000 fee for Optional Practical Training
articles.summary: The Trump administration is reportedly considering imposing a $100,000 fee on international students seeking Optional Practical Training (OPT) authorization to work in the United States after graduating from an American university. This potential policy change was reported by The Wall Street Journal, citing sources familiar with the matter.
articles.insight:
This reported proposal signals heightened regulatory risk for US-bound international students, potentially dampening demand—especially among cost-sensitive applicants from Asia and Latin America—though its actual implementation remains uncertain and subject to legal and political hurdles.  
Admissions teams should track official USCIS updates and consult immigration counsel while benchmarking competitor messaging on post-study work pathways, particularly in markets where OPT has historically influenced destination choice.

articles.title: US universities sell opportunity. A $100k OPT fee could change the product
articles.summary: The Trump administration is considering imposing a $100,000 fee for Optional Practical Training (OPT), a program that allows international students to work in the U.S. after graduation. Richard T. Herman warns that this proposed fee poses a serious risk to U.S. international education.
articles.insight:
This proposed $100,000 OPT fee—though unconfirmed and subject to regulatory hurdles—could dampen U.S. appeal for international students weighing post-study work value, especially from cost-sensitive markets, potentially shifting demand toward countries with more predictable or affordable pathways.  
Admissions teams should track official USCIS updates, consult agents on early sentiment shifts in key source regions like India and China, and benchmark competitor messaging around career outcomes—not as an immediate trigger, but as part of ongoing risk-informed recruitment planning.

articles.title: Nobel-winning chemist criticizes visa curbs as he relocates from US to China
articles.summary: Nobel Prize-winning chemist Omar Yaghi has criticized increasingly restrictive visa policies in the United States and other Western countries. He cited these policies as undermining international scientific collaboration and is relocating from the US to China.
articles.insight:
This high-profile relocation signals potential reputational risk for Western countries’ academic openness, possibly influencing prospective students’ perceptions of visa accessibility and research climate—though direct impact on enrolment decisions remains uncertain and likely mediated by broader geopolitical and economic factors.  
Admissions teams should monitor sentiment shifts in key source markets—especially China—through student surveys and agent feedback, and assess whether visa processing delays or policy rhetoric are increasingly cited as deterrents during application counselling.

articles.title: London’s Bloomsbury Institute loses licence to sponsor international students
articles.summary: The Bloomsbury Institute in London has had its licence to sponsor international students revoked by the UK Home Office. This decision follows the institute’s failure to meet the Basic Compliance Assessment requirements.
articles.insight:
This revocation signals heightened UK regulatory scrutiny of smaller private providers, potentially reinforcing perceptions among international students—especially from risk-averse markets—that institutional reputation and compliance robustness are critical when choosing destinations. It may indirectly influence demand shifts toward more established universities, though broader trends depend on how widely similar enforcement actions spread.  
Admissions teams should monitor UK Home Office updates on sponsor licence suspensions and track student sentiment surveys in key source markets for signs of growing concern about visa reliability or institutional credibility, while reviewing their own compliance documentation readiness.

articles.title: US student visas plunge 62% for Indians, only 34% for Chinese in 2025
articles.summary: In 2025, US student visa issuances to Indian nationals fell by 62 percent, while those to Chinese nationals declined by 34 percent. A think tank’s analysis recommends overhauling the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program, which many Indian graduates rely on for temporary US employment.
articles.insight:
The sharp decline in US student visas for Indian nationals—far exceeding China’s drop—may reflect tightening US immigration policies, growing concerns over post-study work access, or shifting preferences toward alternative destinations, though it remains unclear how much this signals broader demand erosion versus temporary policy-driven disruption.  
Admissions teams should track real-time application trends from India and China, assess how OPT uncertainty affects yield rates, and review messaging around career pathways—particularly for STEM fields—while avoiding premature assumptions about long-term market shifts.
